analysis.one_liner: Taxes every cigarette vending machine $1,000 a year to fund CDC anti-smoking programs.
analysis.headline: Introduced with zero cosponsors on September 25, 1990, the bill was referred to two House committees and never received a vote before the 101st Congress ended on January 3, 1991.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would charge the owner of every cigarette vending machine a $1,000 annual tax, with fines up to $5,000 and up to two years in prison for knowingly skipping it [S3]. All the money would go into a new "Reduced Tobacco Use Program Trust Fund" available only to the Centers for Disease Control for programs aimed at cutting smoking and smoking-related disease [S2][S3]. The tax would take effect January 1, 1991, and would be stacked on top of existing tobacco taxes [S3].
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary people, especially children, would gain from fewer cigarette vending machines, since a $1,000-a-year charge per machine would push many operators to remove them — machines are a known easy source of cigarettes for minors [S3]. The CDC would gain a dedicated funding stream for programs targeting the goals of the Healthy People 2000 Report, which aims to reduce smoking and smoking-induced diseases [S2][S3]. Non-smokers exposed to secondhand smoke and taxpayers who bear the public health costs of smoking would also benefit from any drop in smoking rates.
analysis.who_benefits_short: The public, especially children kept away from cigarettes

how_it_helps.text: It makes each cigarette vending machine cost its owner $1,000 per year, which would push many operators to remove machines — removing a sales channel that lets anyone, including children, buy cigarettes without a clerk checking their age.

It routes every dollar raised into a dedicated trust fund available only to the Centers for Disease Control, to fund the tobacco-reduction goals of the Healthy People 2000 Report and programs against smoking-induced disease.
It backs the tax with real teeth: an owner who willfully fails to pay faces a fine of up to $5,000, up to two years in prison, or both, per machine per year.

analysis.who_pays: The people and businesses that own or operate cigarette vending machines would pay the $1,000 annual tax per machine, and tobacco companies would likely lose sales as machines come out of bars, restaurants, and other locations [S3]. Some of the cost would probably be passed to adult smokers who buy from machines, in higher prices or the inconvenience of finding another source [S3].
analysis.who_pays_short: Vending machine owners and tobacco sellers

drawbacks.text: The cost would fall heavily on small vending route operators, for whom $1,000 per machine per year could exceed the profit a single machine generates — effectively forcing many out of the cigarette machine business rather than just raising revenue.

The penalty is severe for a tax violation: a willful failure to pay carries up to a $5,000 fine and two years of imprisonment per machine per year, raising the stakes well beyond what a civil tax penalty would impose.
Adult smokers who lawfully buy cigarettes from machines would lose convenient access and might pay more as remaining operators pass the tax through to prices.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The public health upside is real but indirect: the tax is designed to make machines uneconomical rather than to raise much money, so its main effect is removing a source of cigarettes that children can buy unattended, with the proceeds funding CDC anti-smoking work [S3]. The cost is concentrated and heavy on the small businesses that own the machines, and the criminal penalty for nonpayment is unusually steep for a tax measure [S3]. On balance the bill trades a concentrated loss for a broad public gain, which is exactly why the machine operators and the tobacco trade would have fought it.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was sent to two House committees, then to a health subcommittee, and no committee ever voted on it before the 101st Congress ended in January 1991, so it died without ever reaching the House floor.

narrative.text: Rep. Pete Stark introduced the bill on September 25, 1990, with no cosponsors.
It was referred the same day to both the House Ways and Means Committee, which handles taxes, and the Energy and Commerce Committee.
On October 8, 1990, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Health and the Environment; no hearing, markup, or floor vote ever followed.
The 101st Congress ended on January 3, 1991, and the bill died in committee.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Cigarette vending machine operators and tobacco companies that sell through machines are better off, since the $1,000 annual tax was never imposed and machine sales continued. The CDC's anti-smoking programs never received the new funding.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Vending machine operators and tobacco sellers

sides.party_line_note: The bill had a single Democratic sponsor and no cosponsors of either party, and it never came to a vote, so no party split can be measured.

industries.note: Each machine would have cost its owner $1,000 a year, with criminal penalties for nonpayment — enough to make most machines unprofitable and push them out of bars, restaurants, and stores. Their unattended machines are the channel that lets children buy cigarettes without an age check, which is why their business interest runs against the bill's public health aim.

Vending machines are a steady retail outlet for cigarettes; a $1,000 annual charge per machine would shrink that outlet, cutting sales. The bill also funds government campaigns against smoking, which work against cigarette demand more broadly.

The bill creates a dedicated trust fund available only to the CDC to run the tobacco-reduction goals of the Healthy People 2000 Report, giving the agency a new revenue stream tied directly to the vending machine tax.
